issues.title: fix(tools): probe literal path before collapsing unicode spaces
issues.body:
## Repro

Any path whose real on-disk name contains U+00A0 (NBSP) — or U+2000–U+200A, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000 — is unaddressable. Verified against the real resolver with a file named `shot\u00A0name.png`: `resolveReadPath(nbspPath, dir)` returned a nonexistent `shot name.png`, so the file could not be read. Worse, with an ASCII-space sibling `shot name.png` present, the resolver silently returned that sibling's bytes — a data-correctness bug, not just UX. This is the path shared by TUI image attach (`handleImagePathPaste` → `resolveReadPath`), `omp read`, and `@file` mentions; macOS names screenshots with NBSP in non-English locales (e.g. `ru_RU`: `Снимок экрана\u00A0— …`).

## Cause

`packages/coding-agent/src/tools/path-utils.ts` — `expandPath()` ran `normalizeUnicodeSpaces()` unconditionally, rewriting every unicode space to ASCII before `resolveReadPath`/`resolveReadPathAsync` built any candidate. The literal on-disk name was destroyed pre-filesystem, and the existing variant chain (`tryMacOSScreenshotPath` U+202F-before-AM/PM, NFD, curly quote) has no inverse for U+00A0, so the literal was unrecoverable. `resolveToCwd()` → `expandPath()` fed the already-mangled string to both resolvers.

## Fix

- `expandPath` / `resolveToCwd` now take an `ExpandPathOptions` with `collapseUnicodeSpaces` (default `true`), so existing callers are unchanged; the unicode-space collapse is skippable.
- New `readPathCandidates()` helper builds the ordered probe list once for both resolvers: the literal (un-collapsed) resolved path is probed **first**, then the collapsed `resolved`, then the shell-escaped variant.
- `resolveReadPath` and `resolveReadPathAsync` use the helper, so a file whose real name holds NBSP resolves to itself; the collapsed form remains a fallback for the paste-from-web case (ASCII-space file requested via an NBSP path).
- Regression test `test/tools/path-utils-unicode-space.test.ts` covers: lone NBSP file → itself; ASCII sibling present → no substitution (sync + async); paste-from-web fallback preserved; U+202F narrow-no-break-space case.

## Verification

The environment has no `node` binary, so `bun run fix` / `bun check` exit 127 on the `#!/usr/bin/env node` shims for `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `tsgo` — a pre-existing, diff-independent failure that reproduces identically on a clean checkout; the pre-publish gate was skipped for that reason. Equivalents were run directly through `bun`: `oxlint --fix` (clean, no diff), `oxfmt` (clean, no diff), `tsgo -p packages/coding-agent/tsconfig.json --noEmit` (exit 0). Targeted tests: `bun test test/tools/path-utils-unicode-space.test.ts test/tools/path-utils-dotdot-selector.test.ts` → 13 pass / 0 fail. Manual repro before/after: pre-fix returned the wrong/nonexistent file, post-fix returns the requested NBSP file's bytes (`RIGHT-FILE`) with and without the ASCII sibling.

Fixes #12805

issues.title: fix(natives): type into macOS Screen Sharing and iPhone Mirroring with the keyboard layout's keys
issues.body:
## What

I work on other Macs through Screen Sharing and on my phone through iPhone Mirroring, and the agent couldn't type into either from the background: it refused, or the other side got a row of `a`s.

**Builds on #15184 and merges after it.**

On macOS the computer tool now types into remote screens with the keys of the user's keyboard layout, so Screen Sharing takes background text, plain keys and holds while the user keeps typing in their own app. Typing into local apps is unchanged from `main`.

| Background action into a Screen Sharing window while the user types in app A | `main` | #15184 | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `type("abc 123 xyz")` | `BackgroundUnavailable` | `BackgroundUnavailable` | lands exactly |
| `type("Abc 123 XyZ")`, `press("cmd+a")` | `BackgroundUnavailable` | `BackgroundUnavailable` | `BackgroundUnavailable`, nothing sent |
| `holdKeys(["x"], {duration: 1})` | `BackgroundUnavailable` | `BackgroundUnavailable` | one keydown, keyup ~1 s later |
| `type("ok 😀")` | refused | refused | `InvalidKey`, nothing sent |
| click a button | A loses focus | passes | passes |
| scroll | passes | passes | passes |
| takeover `type("Abc 123 XyZ")` | a run of `a` | a run of `a` | `Abc 123 XyZ` |

> **macOS context.** Screen Sharing and iPhone Mirroring forward a key event's key code and drop its text. Screen Sharing also takes each forwarded key's modifiers from the physical keyboard, so the background path cannot add one.

Reading order: `keymap.rs` + `keymap-helper.m`, then `keys_for`, `chord_keys`, `type_keys` and `bare_transitions` in `macos/input.rs`, `process::remote_screen`, `report_pointer`.

## Why

Text is mapped through the current layout before anything is sent, so a character no key types refuses whole. Characters in `press` and `holdKeys` take the layout's key too, with the Shift or Option it needs. Remote screens are known by bundle id or by linking Apple's screen-sharing frameworks.

- **Refuse modified background text on Screen Sharing** rather than fake it: holding Shift there would shift the user's own typing.
- **Takeover posts bare key transitions at the HID tap,** checking focus before every press.
- **The layout is read in a helper process** (reused for 10 s): Text Input Sources asserts it runs on the main queue, which the desktop worker is not.
- **Background keys into an app with several windows** recheck before each press that the target is still key, and stop with `InputFailed` otherwise.
- **iPhone Mirroring** gets 120 ms between key transitions, 60 ms taps, and scrolls aimed with a lone mouse-up.

Maintenance: if Apple renames these bundles or frameworks, remote screens fall back to local typing and the rig's `remote-type` case shows a row of `a`.

## Testing

Two macOS VMs: the agent on B drives B's Screen Sharing viewer of A while a USB keyboard types into B's receiver app; a grader checks the user's keys, focus and A's page (`research/omp-coexist/run-matrix.py --cases research/omp-coexist/cases-remote --repeat 3 --commit <ref>`, plus `cases-remote-effect`, `cases-remote-race`). This PR: 3/3 per case above, app A kept focus in every background run.

Residual risk: a modifier the user physically holds at the instant Screen Sharing reads a key would apply to it; with the user typing 78 capitals during 600 background keys, 0 arrived modified.

Each fix has a unit test that fails with it reverted. `cargo nextest run -p pi-natives -E 'test(/desktop::/)'` (143 passed) and `bun run lint:rs` pass; the VM matrix above predates the review fixes (VMs busy).

Not run on a phone: the iPhone Mirroring paths (120 ms gap, taps, scroll aim); the phone was in use. Unit tests and a live classification check cover them.

issues.title: fix: attach lowercase macOS screenshot names
issues.body:
## Problem
macOS screenshot filenames on some systems use lowercase `am`/`pm` after a narrow no-break space. `resolveToCwd` normalizes Unicode spaces, but `tryMacOSScreenshotPath` only restored the narrow space for uppercase `AM`/`PM`, so pasted lowercase screenshot paths resolved to a nonexistent filename and image attachment failed.

## Fix
Make the AM/PM variant case-insensitive while preserving the captured case. Add an attachment-level regression test using a lowercase `pm` screenshot filename with U+202F stored on disk and an ordinary space in the pasted path.

## Verification
- `bun test packages/coding-agent/test/image-paste-source-path.test.ts` could not load because the `pi_natives` native addon is missing. Building the addon was blocked because CMake could not find Ninja.

issues.title: feat(coding-agent): add opt-in prompt suggestions example
issues.body:
## What

**Contributor statement (translated from the contributor’s Chinese wording):**

> Add the `/suggestions` extension. I frequently chat with AI in the terminal and want it to predict my next message to reduce repetitive typing.

Add an opt-in extension example that predicts a short next user message through `@tiny` and renders it as composer ghost text. Tab accepts the suggestion for editing without submitting it. This does not enable background requests by default for OMP users or change core editor APIs.

**Maintainer decision requested: this example has a known, unresolved secret-obfuscation limitation.** The contributor explicitly requested submitting the PR with the limitation disclosed for maintainer review, rather than expanding this change into core APIs.

## Why

Offer the interaction as a separately loadable example, keeping core behavior unchanged. Related: #6863 implements the similar interaction in core; this PR is an extension-based alternative, not a claim that the feature is absent from the review queue.

## Known limitations requiring maintainer review

- **Do not use this example with `secrets.enabled`.** Extension `agent_end` events contain original, display-ready user/assistant text. Direct `completeSimple` requests do not apply the session obfuscator, so protected original values in recent conversation text can be sent to `@tiny` unredacted, including when the main model only receives placeholders. The current public extension API does not expose the protected side-request path. This is **disclosed, not fixed**, in both the standalone source header and example README. Please decide whether to expose/reuse the core protected side-request path, use the core implementation instead, or decline the example as currently scoped.
- Direct requests also do not apply session-level side-request concurrency controls. Installing the example enables extra requests to the configured `@tiny` provider, which may differ from the main provider. Context is capped at six recent user/assistant text turns and 8,000 characters; tool-result, thinking, image, and injected user blocks are excluded, but ordinary chat text may still be sensitive.
- The example replaces the editor and should not be combined with another editor-replacing extension.
- In IME-safe hardware-cursor layouts with side borders, the native editor cannot paint inline ghost text; the extension preserves native Tab behavior instead of accepting an invisible prediction.

## Review and fixes

An independent reviewer inspected the extension and underlying runtime contracts before submission. Three findings were fixed and re-reviewed:

1. Keep credential affinity on the live session but isolate prediction transport identity from the main provider conversation.
2. Do not offer or accept invisible ghost text in affected IME-safe layouts.
3. Do not treat terminal protocol replies or SGR mouse reports as typing that cancels predictions.

A live smoke check also caught and fixed stale `disabled` status after `/suggestions on`. The reviewer confirmed that status transition change. The secret-obfuscation gap above remains intentionally unresolved for maintainer handling.

## Testing

Sanitizer follow-up (`94d7d55b9`): reused the centralized `sanitizeText` and removed partial ANSI/control stripping. Three new regressions failed before the fix and now pass: OSC hyperlinks (BEL/ST), lone surrogates, and Unicode safety at the clipping boundary. Direct runtime probes and an actual OMP extension-load smoke also passed.

Prompt-extraction follow-up (`e3ea815b5`): both prompts are static Markdown text imports, with shared Handlebars compilation for conversation turns. Exact pre/post prompt comparison passed for the system prompt and three user-prompt cases. A standalone copy of the extension plus both templates was loaded and exercised in the actual OMP TUI.

- New real-editor regressions against the original extension: **15 passed, 3 failed**, reproducing the three reviewer findings.
- Fixed extension regression suite: **22 passed, 0 failed**.
- `bun test packages/coding-agent/test/prompt-suggestions-extension.test.ts packages/tui/test/editor.test.ts`: **194 passed, 0 failed**, 667 assertions.
- `bun --cwd=packages/coding-agent run check:types`: passed.
- Targeted `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` on the new extension and test: passed.
- Actual OMP 18.2.0 TUI loaded the PR extension and generated suggestions through the configured `@tiny`: observed gray ghost text becoming normal editable text after CSI-u Tab, without starting a turn; Enter discarded a ghost without submitting it; off/on commands and the corrected idle status were verified.
- Full repository `bun check` and Rust checks were not run. No Rust/core implementation changes are included.

AI assistance was used for implementation, tests, and review. The local interaction was exercised by the contributor before requesting upstream submission; the final PR build was additionally exercised by the coding agent as described above.

issues.title: fix(computer): resolve wayland keyboard input through the active layout
issues.body:
## Repro
In a KDE Wayland session with the French (AZERTY) keyboard layout, `computer.press("a")` inserts `q`, `computer.type("azerty123")` inserts `qwerty&é"`, and `computer.type("é")` fails with `InputFailed: libei cannot type character 'é' with the announced evdev keymap`. Compiling the active `fr` layout with libxkbcommon and comparing it to the crate's fixed US table reproduces the mismatch directly:

```
press("a"): crate sends US evdev 30 -> French layout types 'q' (want evdev 16)
type("é"): US table -> REJECTED (InputFailed); French layout evdev 3
```

## Cause
`crates/pi-natives/src/desktop/linux/wayland/libei.rs` mapped every character through a hardcoded US table (`evdev_char`) and emitted those physical evdev keycodes via `type_text`/`evdev_keycode`. The compositor re-interprets physical keycodes under the *announced* layout, so on AZERTY the US positions produce the wrong glyphs, and any character absent from the US table (`é`, …) was rejected. The `ei_keyboard.keymap` the portal announces was never consulted — the error message referencing it was misleading. The X11 backend already resolves through the active keymap, confirming this was an incomplete implementation.

## Fix
- Add `crates/pi-natives/src/desktop/linux/wayland/xkb.rs`: compile the announced XKB keymap with libxkbcommon and precompute, for every producible Unicode character, the evdev keycode plus the evdev modifier keycodes (Shift, AltGr/`Mod5`→RightAlt, …) that select it. libxkbcommon is loaded at runtime via `dlopen` and never linked, so cross targets that cannot satisfy `-lxkbcommon` (musl, arm64) keep building — mirroring why the PipeWire dependency is opt-in.
- `libei.rs` reads the keymap fd on keyboard `DeviceResumed`, and `type_text`/`key_chord` resolve `KeyName::Char` through the layout, pressing all required modifiers around each keystroke.
- The fixed US table remains only as a fallback for control characters (newline/tab, which XKB reports as non-Unicode keysyms) and when no keymap or libxkbcommon is available; an unresolvable character now reports an accurate error.

## Verification
libxkbcommon-backed resolution was verified against the real `fr` layout (compiled from `xkeyboard-config`), reproducing the exact reported symptoms and confirming the fix: `a`→evdev 16, `A`→16+Shift(42), `é`→evdev 3, `1`→2+Shift, `#`→4+AltGr(100), `@`/`{`/`[`/`|`→AltGr. The new `modifier_evdev` unit tests pass (`Shift`=42, `Mod5`=100, lock modifiers rejected). Live end-to-end validation on a Wayland compositor was not possible in the build environment (no RemoteDesktop portal / libei runtime).

Skipped pre-publish gate: `bun run fix`/`bun check`/`bun run test` cannot run in this environment — `node` is absent so `fix:ts` (oxlint/oxfmt) exits 127, and the native crate's unrelated `zstd-sys`/`opusic-sys` build scripts need a writable cache and `cmake`. Both failures are environmental and independent of this Rust-only change; `rustfmt` was run manually on the touched files.

Fixes #12534

issues.title: perf(tui): bound the final stop's history flush to the newest rows
issues.body:
## What

Quitting a long session took most of a minute, because the final flush wrote out the whole session; now it writes only the newest rows.

`TUI.stop(options?: TUIStopOptions)` takes the shutdown flush's shape. A capped stop, `{ maxRows: EXIT_FLUSH_MAX_ROWS }` (2,000), hands native scrollback only the newest whole blocks that fit (the newest block whole when it alone is taller): `TranscriptContainer.peekFlushBatch(width, maxRows)` measures back from the end of the eligible prefix, never starts inside a block, renders only that tail, and still retires the whole prefix on acknowledgement. A stop without options is an exiting stop and asks the owner's `TUI.setExitFlushProvider()`, as do postmortem restores other than a signal: `InteractiveMode` caps only a *saved* session whose file is still being written, so `omp --resume` restores the skipped messages; an unsaved session (`--no-session`, or one not yet written to disk), a failed teardown or a latched disk failure keeps the full flush. A signal or a terminal disconnect is always capped, since the terminal is gone or a kill usually follows.

Separately, a handoff that resumes with `start()` (suspend, and the external/todo/plan/hook/annotation editors) now passes `{ resuming: true }`, which flushes nothing while a fullscreen overlay holds the screen — it resumes back into that overlay, nothing is committed, and pressure retires the same rows once the overlay closes. That removes a 15-29 s stall previously seen on Ctrl+G and Ctrl+Z from the viewport on a long session. The flush now also ends with `endHistoryFlush()`; the composer had never cleared its flush state, so every frame after a resumed handoff retired every settled block at once instead of by pressure.

## Why

The final stop's flush rendered every un-retired block with no budget. On a long session that meant tens of seconds at quit: 40 s after a fullscreen overlay had held the screen (410,976 rows), 18.7 s on a plain inline `/exit`, and 65.6 s on `SIGTERM` — past the process's own 10 s postmortem deadline, so a killed session could still be mid-flush when the OS gave up waiting on it.

**Placement:** the same red-team that reviewed a related terminal-handoff fix looked at this one too — the flush's lack of a budget is omp's own machinery, not something our deployment configures around, and upstream's own fullscreen overlays (btw, plan review, agent and model hubs) hit the same suspended-retirement stall, so the fix is not fork-specific. A third approach (clearing the transcript from an extension) was considered and rejected: it has no signal-exit coverage, does not fix the resume hint, and is the wrong layer for a structural retirement-budget problem.

## Testing

- `bun check` (lint, format, TS types across every package, `cargo check` across every crate) passes at this head (ebd08138).
- Unit: `packages/tui` `transcript-container`, `history-frame-plan`, `image-budget`, `emergency-restore-altscreen` and `process-terminal-render` pass (144 cases), and `packages/coding-agent/test/startup-composer.test.ts` passes (21), including the fatal-error, failed-teardown, disk-failure and hangup restore cases. Across the 36 coding-agent teardown and interactive-mode test files, 331 pass; the 2 `rpc-shutdown-persistence` tests were killed at their timeout on a heavily loaded machine (load1 around 150-167), the same on the previous head.
- Randomized checks over 2,883 and 2,000 transcript layouts (text, empty and direct-placement image blocks, partly and fully emitted streamed heads, caps from 1 to 40) confirm every capped batch is a whole-block suffix that keeps each image's reserved rows and each separator; the bytes written by 60 stop scenarios without those cases are identical to the previous head.
- I exercised the built CLI directly in a private tmux server against a synthetic 3,000-turn session, in both viewport and normal display modes: `/exit` and literal Ctrl+D each exit 0 with terminal flags restored and the resume hint as the last non-blank scrollback line, and Ctrl+G from the viewport opens the editor in 0.27 s (load1 around 133).
- Before this fix landed on the fork, a separate acceptance pass measured the effect directly on a saved session with a long un-retired transcript: quitting after a fullscreen overlay held the screen dropped from a 26.8-40.9 s median (31.10 s) to 2.12-2.56 s (2.54 s median); a plain inline `/exit` 30 s into the session dropped from a 16.90-24.70 s median (19.89 s) to 1.62-2.30 s (2.30 s); Ctrl+G from the viewport dropped from a ~23 s stall to 0.010 s median, and Ctrl+Z from ~23 s to 0.0084 s. The hint landed as the last scrollback line in every measured run (details and raw figures in that pass's report, not reproduced here since it predates this rebase).

This PR is independent of a related PR that drains or drops queued terminal output at the same handoff (touching the same `TUI.stop()`); whichever of the two merges second will need a rebase over the other's changes to that method.

issues.title: test: restore omp-shell snapshots orphaned by the crate rename
issues.body:
Fixes #12102.

Two orphaned-file failures on a clean checkout, one cause each. 213 files, **+2 lines** — 211 of them are pure renames.

## 211 orphaned shell snapshots

The crate was renamed `omp-shell-engine` → `omp-shell`. insta derives a snapshot's filename from the crate name, so every tracked `.snap` stopped being found:

```
in git:      omp_shell_engine__parser__program__tests__…
insta looks:  omp_shell__parser__program__tests__…
```

These were **not** unapproved snapshots — that is why each failure showed only a `+new` side with no `-old` to diff against. `cargo insta accept` would have "fixed" them while silently discarding whatever the tracked originals asserted.

**Renamed, not re-accepted.** Every body was first proven byte-identical to its tracked original, comparing only the content below the YAML front matter:

```
identical=211   differing=0   unpaired=0
```

The single difference is the `source:` header, which still points at `brush-parser/` — the upstream path this parser was ported from. Had even one body differed, the mass rename would have been hiding a real parser regression, so the gate ran first and its result is the reason this is a rename commit rather than an accept.

`omp-shell`: **355/355**.

## A fixture that excluded itself from git

`crates/tools/tests/fixtures/special-sources` exists to prove `read` honours `.gitignore`, so it needs files git really ignores. Its own `.gitignore` lists them — so git ignored them for real and they were never committed. `manifest.json` declares them and `special_source_fixture_workspace_is_complete_and_self_contained` asserts they exist, so the test failed on any clean checkout.

Now tracked via `git add -f`, with the reason recorded at the top of the fixture's `.gitignore` so they are not later mistaken for stray build output.

## Workspace state

8858/8877 after these repairs. The remaining 19 are pre-existing and unrelated to this change:

| n | cause |
|---:|---|
| 2 | `touch::` needs `atime`; this volume is APFS mounted `noatime` — cannot pass on macOS |
| 1 | load-sensitive timeout (`fast_output_is_host_bounded…`), passes unloaded |
| 16 | extension-host and edit-engine contract failures, needing their own analysis |

No failures in `omp-shell` or in the fixture test.

issues.title: feat(coding-agent/prompts): route bulk chunk transforms through eval map-reduce
issues.body:
## What

- Add a `<map-reduce>` block to `prompts/tools/eval.md`: slice a long input inside the kernel, run one `completion(model="smol")` per slice via `parallel`, aggregate in code. Worked example per runtime (Python / JS).
- State that large sources load through in-kernel `read(path)` (paginated by offset/limit), never the outer `read` tool's `:raw`/whole-file form, so the source stays a kernel-only handle instead of being spent on the turn's context.
- Add a delegation-gate bullet in `prompts/system/system-prompt.md` routing bulk per-item semantic work to that in-kernel pattern instead of subagent fan-out, gated on the eval tool being present.
- CHANGELOG entry under `[Unreleased]` / `Changed`.

## Why

The eval prelude already exposes `completion()` and `parallel()`, but the prompts documented only the subagent DAG pattern, so per-chunk semantic work over a long input got verbalized as `tasks[]` batches. Verbalized delegation cannot express fan-out over hundreds of slices, and the concurrency cap makes `task` the wrong instrument for it.

Design follows Recursive Language Models ([arXiv:2512.24601](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24601)), which measures both effects this change targets: in-context decomposition examples improve first-decomposition quality and final scores, and programmatic sub-calls beat verbalized delegation on information-dense work (58.0 vs 28.4 F1 on OOLONG-Pairs).

## Verification

Prompt-guidance changes have no unit-testable contract, so this was verified behaviorally against a locally compiled binary (`bun run build`, `--smoke-test` exit 0), driving `claude-sonnet-5` as root with `claude-haiku-4-5` as the smol tier, `-p --mode=json` transcripts parsed for the real tool-call sequence.

**Trigger case** — classify all 1129 `CHANGELOG.md` bullets into 6 subsystems (semantic per-item work, ~64k tokens of input):

- Routed to `parallel([... completion(model="smol") ...])`, 57 batches × 20 items. 57 `completion()` invocations confirmed from eval cell status events, not source inspection.
- **1129/1129 classified** — total matches ground truth exactly, so no chunk silently dropped.
- Zero `task` subagents spawned.

**Negative control** — count issue/PR citations in the same file (mechanically computable, so sub-calls would be waste):

- `bash`×2, `grep`×4, `eval`×10 (pure regex/`Counter`), **zero `completion()` calls** — the routing bullet does not over-trigger onto work that plain code should do.
- Answer (228 citing bullets / 223 distinct / 11 repeated) independently recomputed and byte-matched.

**Before/after on the `:raw` line** — same prompt and models, re-run after adding that one sentence:

| | without the line | with it |
|---|---|---|
| outer `read` `:raw` calls | 3 (~24k tokens into root context) | 0 |
| content loading | `:raw` ×3, then `cat`→`/tmp`→`open()` | in-kernel `read()` from the start |
| `completion()` invocations | 57 | 57 |
| run cost | $0.43 | $0.26 |

Routing behavior held constant; the ~24k tokens of avoidable whole-file reads is what disappeared.

**Static checks:** `bun test` across the 7 `system-prompt*` files plus `prompt-templates`, both `eval-description*`, and `eval-code-mode-declarations` — 144 pass / 8 skip / 0 fail. ## What

Split out of #11207 at the maintainer's request ([comment](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/pull/11207#issuecomment-5912083587)). That PR bundled four independent changes; this is **part 3 of 4, the `/advisor config` editor and the per-advisor status glyphs**. The maintainer listed four changes: advisor-off inheritance and selective restart on roster apply (points 1 and 2, kept together in #11207), this editor (point 3) and the advisor curator (point 4, #13932).

**Editor.** On `main`, `/advisor config` shows one scope at a time: a roster on the left and the selected advisor on the right. This PR shows both scopes at once, the project roster on the upper left, the global roster on the lower left, and the selected advisor's fields on the right. Each scope has its own `+ Add advisor`, `Shared instructions` and `Save & apply` rows, and `Save & apply` writes that scope's own `WATCHDOG.yml`. The frame below is the real output of the overlay at 110 columns with the unicode symbol preset and `Security` selected; glyphs and key labels follow the active preset. The two scopes were edited one at a time, and the state of each advisor was not visible at a glance.

issues.body:
Brings a few ideas from [Hindsight](https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight) into Mnemopi while keeping it local (SQLite) and cache-safe.

## Retain quality
- Deterministic TR/EN chatter gate before episode writes; the dispose path (which skips the N-turn threshold) no longer stores greeting-only sessions. Retention protocol markers (`[role: user]`, `[user:end]`) are stripped before the check.
- Extraction no longer turns every long line / broken JSON into facts; completed items are salvaged from truncated JSON. Turkish declarative fallback widened.
- Facts carry a `memory_kind` (`world` | `experience`). User turns feed world/preference/instruction extraction; assistant turns go through a separate experience-only prompt, so assistant text can never become a user fact. Idempotent migration; untyped rows default to `world`.

## Evidence-backed observations
- Same fact from distinct sources is reinforced (`proof_count`, `sources_json`) instead of duplicated; `memory_validations` now receives reinforce/weaken entries with source id + quote.
- Conservative supersession: `superseded_by` only on explicit negation or known single-valued predicates (`lives_in`, `works_at`, …). Ambiguous cases stay active.
- Works with `polyphonicRecall` off. Same-source/summary re-ingest doesn't double count or resurrect superseded facts. Purge keeps facts still backed by other sources. Unicode-aware normalization.
- Recall hides superseded facts; small proof boost (alpha 0.1).

## PII redaction
`redactMemorySecrets` adds typed masks for email, TR phone, TCKN (checksum), IBAN (mod-97), card numbers (Luhn) plus a few credential prefixes; credentials are redacted first.

## Tests
`bun test packages/mnemopi/test`: 479 pass. coding-agent memory tests pass; one pre-existing Windows `EBUSY` temp-dir teardown flake in `mnemopi-recall-features.test.ts`. `check:types` clean for both packages. Migration smoke-tested against a copy of a real user DB.

issues.title: docs: document xd:// device protocol and hook observability
issues.body:
## Repro
The `xd://` tool-device transport (`packages/coding-agent/src/tools/xdev.ts`, `internal-urls/xd-protocol.ts`) is actively surfaced — discoverable/MCP/custom tools are mounted as `xd://<tool>` devices and announced via `xdev-mount-notice.md` — but the `omp://` docs corpus documented only the `/xdev/resolve|reject|propose` sub-cases, never the general protocol. Reading `omp://` (or grepping `docs/` for `xd://`) turns up nothing about device mounting or its hook-visible shape. An extension author wiring a `tool_result` hook to intercept a specific MCP tool's output found it never fired when that tool was invoked through `write xd://mcp__tool`, with no doc explaining why.

## Cause
Two gaps, both documentation:
1. No doc describes the `read xd://` / `write xd://<tool>` protocol, the `isMountableUnderXdev` device-vs-first-class rule, or the resulting `toolName`/`input` shape.
2. The observability question was undocumented. Verified in code: every registry tool is wrapped once by `ExtensionToolWrapper` (`extensibility/extensions/wrapper.ts`), the sole emitter of `tool_call`/`tool_result`. A `write xd://<tool>` dispatch runs inside `WriteTool.execute()` via `XdevRegistry.dispatch()` (`tools/xdev.ts:313`), which calls the mounted tool's `execute()` on the **raw, unwrapped** instance (`tools/write.ts:1034`). So the inner dispatch emits no event: hooks see exactly one event with `toolName === "write"`, the device name under `event.input.path`, and the dispatch envelope under `event.details.xdev`.

## Fix
- Add `docs/xd-devices.md`: protocol shape, rationale, `isMountableUnderXdev` mount rule, the hook/extension observability contract (with a working `tool_result` interception example keyed off `write` + `parseXdUrl(event.input.path)`), and the `tools.xdev: false` fallback. Cross-links `hooks.md`, `resolve-tool-runtime.md`, `custom-tools.md`, `mcp-runtime-lifecycle.md`.
- Cross-link the observability note from `docs/hooks.md`'s Tool-events section.

The file is auto-served by `omp://` (docs are globbed from `docs/**/*.md` in `internal-urls/docs-index.ts`).

## Verification
Confirmed `omp://` discovery globs the new file and the intra-doc anchor `#hook--extension-observability` matches GitHub's heading slug (ran the `docs/` glob + slug derivation used by `docs-index.ts`). Traced the dispatch path (`write.ts` → `XdevRegistry.dispatch` → unwrapped `inst.execute`) and the wrapper's single `tool_call`/`tool_result` emission (`wrapper.ts:206,245`) to confirm the documented `toolName="write"` / `event.details.xdev` shape is exact. Documentation-only change; no runtime code touched. Fixes #6105

issues.title: perf(ttsr): resume rule scanning from a bounded offset window
issues.body:
## `checkDelta` re-matched the whole accumulated buffer on every delta

`checkDelta` (`ttsr.ts:512`) appends the delta to the per-stream buffer and passes the **entire accumulated buffer** to `#matchBuffer`, which iterates every rule and calls `#matchesCondition`, running `condition.test(streamBuffer)` from index 0 each time.

That is O(rules × buffer) per delta and O(n²/16 × rules) per stream. The text/thinking asymmetry the issue reports is real: `checkDelta:513-518` early-returns for those two sources when no rule can match them, but `tool` has no such guard, so tool-argument streams take the full path on every delta.

## The fix

Buffers only grow by appending, so a prefix already proven to hold no match stays a valid claim. Each rule now records how far its conditions have scanned, and the next delta resumes at `offset - window`, where `window` bounds how long that condition's match can be.

`maxMatchLength()` computes that bound syntactically and conservatively: repetition (`*`, `+`, `{`), alternation, backreferences, `^`, word boundaries and lookbehind all report unbounded and keep scanning in full, so no matchable text is ever skipped. Sticky lookahead forms — which is what `compileRuleCondition` and `optimizeRuleCondition` produce — are in the full-scan set too, because they may only match at index 0; slicing them would change semantics.

Offsets are cleared wherever the buffer is: `checkSnapshot` (which replaces rather than appends), `resetBuffer`, and `clearStream`. They are tracked per rule rather than per stream, because a rule held back by the repeat gate is skipped on some deltas, and a shared offset would let it skip text it never actually saw.

## Measurement

```
fix applied:  10 pass / 0 fail
source only:   8 pass / 2 fail
  (fail) rescans each delta instead of the whole accumulated buffer
  (fail) keeps bounded rescanning linear as the stream grows
```

The test counts **characters read** by wrapping `RegExp.prototype.test`, rather than measuring wall-clock, so it asserts the quantity the issue is actually about.

16 KiB in 16-byte deltas is 1025 deltas. Current code reads sum(16, 32, …, n) ≈ 8.4M characters; this reads roughly 1025 × (16 + 25) ≈ 42K, which fails the `< deltas * 100` bound by about 80× and passes with about 2.4× headroom. The second case is the scaling one: 8 KiB → 16 KiB currently **quadruples** the total, and the test requires less than 3×.

Eight further cases pin the resume logic rather than the speedup: four exactness cases (a match spanning a delta boundary, a match at buffer start, a match after a long non-matching prefix, and an unbounded `QUIET.+PROFILE` still found at 2000 chars) and four lifecycle cases. Each lifecycle case uses a 77-character filler prefix so a leaked offset provably differs from a cleared one — leaked resumes at 62 and slices to the empty string and misses; cleared starts at 0 and matches.

Those lifecycle cases were rewritten after the first measurement, and the reason matters: my originals asserted outcomes that were impossible on main too, so they could never have discriminated. An assertion that cannot fail is not a regression test.

## Honest limit

The bound is a syntactic over-estimate, so a bounded rule re-reads roughly its own pattern length per delta rather than a minimal window. That is a small constant, not a correctness risk.

Patterns with unbounded quantifiers — common in real kit rules — keep the old full-buffer cost. So this fixes the reported literal-rule case and fixed-width conditions generally, **not every rule**. A debounce or an incremental-matcher-state design would go further; the issue lists those as maintainer tradeoffs rather than prescriptions, so I implemented none of them.

<!-- Error Output: none -->
<!-- Unsafe: no -->
<!-- Major changes: no -->
<!-- CI-Ready: yes, ttsr-delta-scan 10 pass / 0 fail -->
<!-- Platform-Specific: no, wraps RegExp.prototype.test for one synchronous call -->
<!-- Scope Lint: one source file, one new test file, one changelog entry -->

Fixes #14248

issues.title: fix(ai): exempt structured content from thinking-loop heuristics
issues.body:
## Repro
Driving `withThinkingLoopGuard` for a deepseek-class model and streaming a legitimate final answer — a 33-row markdown table plus the requested `[TA_CASES]#{...}` JSON trailer of 33 same-shape items — as visible `text_delta` trips the guard with `Thinking loop detected: the model repeated near-identical content (4 near-identical segments within the last 16)`, exactly the message from the issue. The model is not looping; the answer is complete and correct. In `--mode json` the discarded attempt was auto-retried up to `maxAttempts`, re-streaming the same ~6.6 KB report 9-10 times.

## Cause
`ThinkingLoopDetector` in `packages/ai/src/utils/thinking-loop.ts` force-flushes wall-of-text content (no blank-line boundaries) into `SEGMENT_CHAR_CAP`-sized chunks and runs the near-duplicate word-trigram cluster over them. `normalizeSegment` drops digits, so consecutive table rows / JSON items — whose only variation is numeric ids and URLs — normalize to near-identical trigrams and reach the 4-segment cluster threshold. Those heuristics were calibrated on reasoning prose; homogeneous structured data is legitimate answer content, not a reasoning loop.

## Fix
- Add `proseRatio()` scoring a segment's prose-likeness: Unicode letters + whitespace versus JSON/table punctuation (`STRUCTURAL_PUNCT`), ignoring digits so data identifiers tilt neither side. CJK and other scripts count as prose.
- In `#consumeSegment`, skip segments below `SEGMENT_MIN_PROSE_RATIO` (0.85) before the near-duplicate and lexical-stall paths, and reset any in-progress prose stall on a structured block.
- Exact suffix-cycle detection is untouched, so a verbatim structured loop is still caught; reasoning-prose loops (including after a table) still trip.

## Verification
`bun test packages/ai/test/thinking-loop.test.ts` -> 43 pass / 0 fail, including two new regression tests: a homogeneous markdown-table + JSON-array answer no longer trips, and a reasoning-prose loop following structured output still trips. The end-to-end guard repro that failed before the fix now commits the answer cleanly (`stopReason=stop`). Fixes #11129

issues.title: fix(vcs): contain patch paths to the worktree and refuse the git store
issues.body:
`validate_repo_path` accepted any relative path without `..`. Nothing else checked containment, so patch application had no defence against a path that resolves outside the worktree once symlinks are followed, and none at all against `.git/`.

**Scope, stated honestly:** the patch text reaching `apply_patch` today is either generated internally from `diff_text` or supplied by the user through the git overlay — the model-facing `apply_patch` tool does not route through `omp_vcs`. This is defence in depth, not a live hole. It seemed worth closing before something untrusted is wired to a function that looks safe.

## Six rules

| Rule | What it stops |
|---|---|
| `.git` refused per-component under every filesystem spelling | `.GIT/hooks/pre-commit` opens the real store on case-insensitive mounts; also `GIT~1`, trailing dot/space, and the codepoints HFS+ folds away |
| Store refused by **location**, not just name | `git init --separate-git-dir=meta .` puts the real store in `meta/`, which no name check can recognise |
| Containment checked **before anything is read** | `augment_patch_sources` opens each source to build the state map — a source under an escaping symlink is read from outside the worktree, and aimed at a device or FIFO that read becomes unbounded memory growth or a hang |
| Every side validated up front | A patch whose early files are legitimate and whose later target escapes no longer half-applies; a rename no longer deletes its source before the target is refused |
| Deletion validates the **prefix**, not the leaf | `remove_file` unlinks without following, so a repository legitimately tracking an outbound symlink can still delete, stash, pop and cherry-pick it |
| `cherry_pick` validates **before** `commit_as` | It moved HEAD and only then wrote the worktree, so a refused path left HEAD ahead of an index and worktree that never received the change |

The alias set is applied on every platform rather than under `cfg`: a patch is a portable artifact, and a tree authored on macOS may be applied on Linux from a case-insensitive mount, so the compiling host cannot decide it. The list was verified against `git update-index` rather than transcribed — U+200C, U+200D, U+FEFF and U+206F are rejected by git itself as `Invalid path`; U+2060 is not.

`can_apply_patch` runs the same preflight, so the predicate cannot answer `true` for a patch `apply_patch` then refuses, and cannot be used as a read primitive.

## Residual TOCTOU

Documented at the guard rather than left implicit. The check is not atomic with the write; closing that needs `openat`/`O_NOFOLLOW` descriptor-relative writes which the surrounding code does not use. Accepted because an attacker able to plant directories mid-apply already has workspace write access. What the guard stops is the untrusted patch text.

## Verification

`omp-vcs` 51/51. Twelve regression tests, each **confirmed to fail** against the unfixed code by neutralising its guard in isolation:

```
BITES  case_insensitive_git_aliases
BITES  hfs_ignorable_git_spellings
BITES  read_a_source_through_an_escaping_symlink
BITES  separate_git_dir_store
BITES  cherry_pick_refuses_before_advancing_head
BITES  stash_roundtrip_preserves_outbound_symlink
```

Ported from an equivalent fix reviewed at can1357/oh-my-pi#11375, where nine review findings — including three P1s raised after the first round — were resolved against the same code shape on the `main` branch.

issues.title: fix(natives): stop hashlineIsReadTruncationNotice breaking every PR's CI
issues.body:
## What

Removes the `hashlineIsReadTruncationNotice` napi export and reimplements it as a pure TS port of `crates/pi-edit/src/modes/hashline/prefixes.rs::is_read_truncation_notice` in `packages/coding-agent/src/tools/hashline-format.ts`. The underlying Rust function stays in `pi-edit` (it's still called internally by `is_read_metadata_line`); only the thin `#[napi]` wrapper in `pi-natives` goes away.

I reviewed the full diff and pulled the actual GitHub Actions logs for a currently-running PR (run 34990251125) before writing this: every open PR fails with some variant of "X is not a function" against `@oh-my-pi/pi-natives`, and for `hashlineIsReadTruncationNotice` specifically the cause is a version-sentinel gap, not a build problem.

## Why

`native_addons` on the PR path fetches `@oh-my-pi/pi-natives-linux-x64@latest` from npm instead of building from source (`ci.yml` lines 226-274), by design — "native changes are validated post-merge on main and at release." The push-to-main path that *would* build from source has 0 runs under the current CI workflow ID, so the npm-fetch path is the only signal anyone actually sees pre-merge.

`hashline_is_read_truncation_notice` was added to `pi-natives` in 1d75181e (Sep 11) and immediately consumed by `hashline-format.ts` in the same change. The natives package version (18.2.0) was published to npm before that commit landed and hasn't been re-published since, so the addon PR CI tests against doesn't have the export. I downloaded and inspected the actual published `pi_natives.linux-x64-modern.node`: `vcsDiscover` and `editDescription` (added earlier the same week) are present as symbols, `hashlineIsReadTruncationNotice` is not. The version-sentinel check in `loader-state.js` can't catch this — it's keyed on the package version number, which never moved, so a same-version addon that predates a later commit passes validation silently and the missing export only shows up as a runtime crash.

This is the same failure mode fixed four days earlier in 95337cf2 for `edit_description_compact` ("PR CI tests against the latest release .node by design... Static prompt text needs no native boundary; import the markdown directly and drop the napi export"). `is_read_truncation_notice` is a ~15-line pure string classifier with no OS/perf dependency, so the same fix applies.

Confirmed via the actual CI job log (job 104453116692, `Test coding-agent UI/TUI (TS)`):
```
TypeError: hashlineIsReadTruncationNotice is not a function. (In 'hashlineIsReadTruncationNotice(line)', 'hashlineIsReadTruncationNotice' is undefined)
```

issues.title: feat: name the repo in issue/PR refs and hyperlink #N and owner/repo#N
issues.body:
## What

Enable links for GitHub issues and PRs to make it easier to navigate from the CLI to them.

Refine issue/PR-like linking in omp by having the model be more specific about what it's talking about + a linker to cover most cases. Safe defaults and behavior is preserved where possible.

End to end, issue/PR references in assistant replies now say which repo they belong to, and they open that repo's issue or PR when clicked:

1. **The model writes references that name the repo.** A system-prompt rule: bare `#N` means the cwd repo only. Refs to any other repo (forks and upstreams included) must be `owner/repo#N`, or a full URL for hosts other than GitHub.
2. **The TUI turns them into terminal hyperlinks (OSC 8).** The visible text stays exactly `#3460` or `owner/repo#12`, and no URL is printed.
   - `owner/repo#N` links to `https://github.com/owner/repo/issues/N`. GitHub redirects that to the PR when N is a PR.
   - Bare `#N` links to the cwd's github.com repo: the same `gh` default repo that `pr://N` and `issue://N` use (`tryResolveCurrentRepo`). With no GitHub repo, or no `gh`, bare refs stay plain.
   - Not linked: code spans and blocks, existing link labels (a nested OSC 8 would replace the link's href), refs attached to other text (`C#3`, `file.ts#4`, `a/b/c#5`, `#6x`, `#0`), `.`/`..` repo names (`a/..#2` would resolve outside `a`), and all-digit hex colours such as `#111111`, which keep their swatch.
   - With `tui.hyperlinks: off`, or a terminal without OSC 8, the output is byte-identical plain text.

## Why

`#N` in chat output usually refers to the current repo's issue tracker, and reaching it meant copying the number and building the URL by hand.

Models also write `#N`, or a Markdown link built from the cwd repo, for items that live elsewhere: a fork's upstream, a dependency. The link then opens the wrong issue. The renderer cannot tell which repo a bare `#N` meant, so the fix has two halves. The prompt rule makes the model name the repo whenever it isn't the cwd one. The linker keeps bare `#N` clickable for the common case and makes the new `owner/repo#N` form clickable too, so the rule does not cost users links.

Refs are not rewritten into Markdown links because the `link` renderer prints `text (url)`, which would add the URL to every reference.

This supersedes #13523, which carried the prompt rule and a smaller linker.

## How

- `system-prompt.md`: one line under `<evidence-and-output>`.
- `MarkdownTheme.githubRepo` (pi-tui): the leaf `text` case of `Markdown.#renderInlineTokens` wraps matches with `formatHyperlink`. Text between matches still goes through `renderTextWithSwatches`. Link labels render with `inLink` set, so refs inside them stay plain.
- `assistant-message.ts`: each `AssistantMessageComponent` takes a reader for the GitHub repo of the session that rendered it, so invalidation never moves an existing message to another repo. The prose theme is rebuilt on invalidation, so render caches keyed on theme identity pick up a newly resolved repo.
- `InteractiveMode.proseGithubRepo(at?)`: resolves the repo of `viewSession`'s cwd in the background, so a focused agent links to its own repo. It keeps each session's cwd history, keyed by session id, and resolves bare `#N` against the repo of the cwd at the reply's timestamp. A resolved repo invalidates the UI, and rendering never waits on it.
- `ChatTranscriptBuilder`: the rewind and copy transcript replays receive the same reader.
- Ref boundaries are Unicode-aware, and a trailing `/` disqualifies a ref.

## Testing

- `packages/tui/test/markdown.test.ts`, 6 new tests:
  - bare and qualified refs with unchanged visible text
  - no repo, so only qualified refs link
  - code, link labels, attached-text (`café#11`, `#12é`, `a/b#13/c`) and `.`/`..` negatives
  - hex colour swatch precedence
  - hyperlinks disabled
  - streaming byte identity

  The positive and swatch tests fail when the renderer change is reverted. The `a/..#9`/`a/.#10` negatives fail without the `.`/`..` guard.
- `packages/tui/test/assistant-message-github-refs.test.ts`: two messages with different session repos keep their own links across invalidation. It fails if the repo is shared between messages again.
- `packages/coding-agent/test/interactive-mode-prose-github-repo.test.ts`: a reply rebuilt after a cwd change keeps the repo it was written in, and a resumed session's older replies use that session's repo.
- On current `main`: `packages/tui` `bun test`, 2844 pass, 0 fail. `packages/coding-agent` `bun test test/prompt-templates.test.ts`, 53 pass, 0 fail.
- `bun run check:ts` passes. `oxfmt` is clean on touched files.
- The rule appears in the system prompt rendered by `omp --mode rpc` (`get_state`).
- Smoke test in a real checkout: `tryResolveCurrentRepo` returned `can1357/oh-my-pi`, and an `AssistantMessageComponent` emitted `can1357/oh-my-pi/issues/3460` for `#3460` with the visible text unchanged.

A companion ompweb change links the same references in the web UI: kahme247/ompweb#131.

issues.body:
## What

The status line git segment now shows upstream divergence next to the branch: `⇡N` commits ahead and `⇣M` commits behind, rendered before the dirty indicators (`*`/`+`/`?`):

```
 π  · ◉ k3 · 🗑 omp-ab-demo · ⑂ main ⇡1 ⇣2 *1 ?1 · ◫ 2.2%/1M ⟲
```

## How

- **pi-vcs**: `StatusSummary` gains `ahead`/`behind` (`Option<u32>`). The git backend resolves the branch's configured upstream from `branch.<name>.remote`/`.merge` and counts divergence with a gix rev-walk (`with_hidden`); reftable repos fall back to `git rev-list --left-right --count`. Branches without an upstream, detached/unborn HEAD, and jj workspaces report `None`, so nothing renders for them.
- **napi**: `VcsStatusSummary` passes both fields through (`ahead?`/`behind?`).
- **status line**: git segment renders `⇡`/`⇣` (theme icons `icon.ahead`/`icon.behind`, with `^`/`v` under the ascii symbol preset), toggleable via `statusLine.segmentOptions.git.showAheadBehind` (default on; off in the minimal preset).

- coding-agent: `status-line-git-upstream.test.ts` covers indicator ordering, nonzero-only rendering, in-sync/absent suppression, `showAheadBehind: false`, and the ascii preset fallback.

issues.body:
## What

Add optional Gemini Live sessions to the existing `/live` and RPC surfaces. Codex remains the default; choosing Gemini for Live does not change the selected main coding model.

- Google AI Studio API-key login through `/login google`, `omp login google`, and auth-broker login, using the existing credential store and masked secret input. Auth policy remains in catalog KDL.
- Gemini Live voice/thinking configuration, PCM input/playback, independent user transcripts, mute/barge-in, and asynchronous function calls.
- Direct JavaScript/Python execution through the session's allowed Eval tool, without sending every command to the main model. Heavier tasks can still be delegated to the selected coding model.
- Opt-in direct computer control through the existing native desktop surface. Both `live.computer` and `computer.enabled` must be enabled; screenshots go to Google, actions affect the real desktop, and session permissions still apply. This is local host execution, not a Google code sandbox.
- Explicit cancellation for owned direct/delegated work, terminal results for cancelled function IDs, and cancellation of Gemini-owned coding work when Live stops. Unrelated coding work and Codex's ordinary-stop behavior are preserved.
- Paced, bounded microphone sends and compressed screenshot results that retain their coordinate dimensions. Under congestion, stale unsent audio is dropped; a screenshot that cannot fit is omitted with a warning.
- Google Live's default model now comes from catalog KDL and generated rules; `live.google.model` remains an override.
- Recoverable direct-tool errors are shown locally without stopping Live, with call IDs/function names in logs and connection-key redaction.
- Live text input: `m` opens a message field, Enter sends directly to the Live model even while muted, and Esc closes the field without ending Live. Native terminal editing and ANSI input use the same draft/send state.
- Desktop guidance explicitly uses the global `wait(...)`, checks existing windows before launching, and requires inspecting partial effects before retrying rather than repeating completed launches.

No native/Rust source changes, Win32 typing-pacing changes, new dependencies, or fork-only verification workflows are included.

## Why

omp is a great tool, and one of the things that makes it great is that it is model-agnostic. You recently introduced the Live feature, which I loved, but it requires a Codex subscription. I’m proposing that we use an existing free solution to introduce model-agnostic Live mode too. I mean, come on—that honestly sounds cool!

I'd like Live to offer the same provider choice as the rest of omp. I'm including direct execution and opt-in computer control so Gemini can handle straightforward requests itself, while the independently selected main model remains available for heavier coding and reasoning.

Google's [Gemini API pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing) currently lists this Live model as free on the Free Tier. Eligibility, [quotas](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits), and Google's data-use terms apply; availability/pricing can change. Paid-tier use and delegated coding can cost separately. This is not unlimited or permanently free access.

## Testing

Latest verification ran locally on **Windows x64 only**, using Bun 1.4.2.

**Real-provider status:** the newest stored Google login answered a typed prompt with “Typed input works” while the microphone was muted, with no tools or main-model calls. Earlier project-access rejection probes used a separate environment fallback credential and do not establish a ban on that login. An explicit direct-execution arithmetic request still received Gemini's spoken “system error” without a client-side tool call; that provider/model behavior remains unresolved. The user separately observed Chrome launching before `desktop.wait(...)` failed. The desktop guidance is corrected and the supported global waits were exercised, but the Chrome launch was not repeated.

- **55 focused tests passed, 0 failed** across 8 files after integrating text input: Live widget, transport/controller/execution/settings, RPC, and the Live command controller. Coverage includes muted text sends, field Esc versus call Esc, pending/failed drafts, native replacement edits, and late/interrupted microphone turn boundaries.
- An actual Windows PTY **M → text field → Enter → Live controller → loopback websocket → real Eval** smoke computed `82` with zero main-model calls and kept the microphone muted. Sending Esc returned to the normal muted Live controls without ending the call; the terminal surface was inspected and closed cleanly.
- Native read-only desktop execution exercised both `await wait(20)` and predicate waiting, returning `42` without launching apps, sending input, or taking screenshots.
- Real Google text conversation was exercised with the newest saved login selected only for the isolated probe. No credential rows or user configuration were changed. Codex text uses the existing <=500-byte Frameless Bidi context appends; its real-provider conversational response remains unverified.
- `bun run check:ts` passed repository lint, formatting, and all package TypeScript checks. After tightening enhanced-keyboard M handling, repository lint/formatting and the TUI package type check passed again.
- A second actual Windows terminal smoke exercised Kitty-protocol M and Esc, submitted a draft with zero mute toggles, and returned to the muted controls without ending Live. Its focused regression failed before the enhanced-key fix and passed afterward; all six widget tests passed.
- The rebuilt Windows x64 baseline executable `omp-windows-x64-live-text.exe` returned `omp/18.6.0` and passed `--smoke-test` (`smoke-test: ok`). It was built under a separate filename so the user's running executable/session remained untouched.

Earlier verification for the preceding auth/catalog/direct-execution changes:

- A real Windows PTY smoke exercised **Live command UI → controller → loopback websocket → actual Eval**: a failing JavaScript cell surfaced a redacted, tab-sanitized error while Live stayed listening; a replacement cell computed `82`, with zero main-model calls. The terminal output was inspected and the session closed cleanly.

## What

- Add a final `tool_authorization` extension event after every `tool_call` input rewrite and before TUI or ACP approval.
- Provide the exact execution input, native allow or ask decision, approval mode, and whether explicit policy or provider safety requires a human.
- Compose extension decisions by strictness: deny, then ask, then allow. Fail closed on errors, timeouts, cancellation, and unsupported decisions.
- Preserve explicit per-tool prompts and provider safety checks even when an extension returns allow.
- Route extension-only asks through ACP `requestPermission` when form elicitation is unavailable, including explicit yolo and `autoApprove` sessions, while routine auto-approved calls still bypass the native permission gate.
- Require a fresh ACP prompt for each extension ask even when the user previously selected `allow_always`.
- Include the sanitized, width-bounded extension reason in ACP permission requests and report form-less ACP sessions as headless to extensions.
- Shorten extension paths in user-visible final authorization failures.

## Why

Extensions can currently inspect and rewrite tool calls, but they cannot make a final authorization decision over the exact input that will execute. This event provides that last decision point without weakening native safety requirements.

issues.title: feat(mcp): per-server enabledTools/disabledTools tool filtering - Copilot/Claude/OpenCode/Qwen/Anigravity parity
issues.body:
# feat(mcp): per-server enabledTools/disabledTools tool filtering (picomatch)

## What

Per-server, tool-level filtering for MCP servers: `enabledTools` / `disabledTools` in the server config. A server now contributes only the chosen subset of its advertised tools to the model context — persistently, across every session.

```jsonc
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "slack": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.slack.com/mcp",
      "enabledTools": ["search", "read", "channel_*"],
      "disabledTools": ["schedule_message", "create_*"]
    }
  }
}
```

## Why — context cost

Tool schemas are context: measured MCP tool definitions cost ~300–1,000 tokens each (MCP issue #2808: ~1,000/tool heavy, ~100/tool light; community averages 300–600/tool, 515/tool in a 106-tool MySQL server — 54,604 tokens on every initialization). Hosted servers ship toolsets users only partially need:

- Goose (Block) ships a per-extension `available_tools` allowlist and documents "Goose recommends limiting tools to 25" for the GitHub MCP server's ~40 tools (block/goose#2927) — same problem, same answer.
- A 45-tool server: ~13.5K–45K tokens ≈ 7–22% of a 200K window per session.
- Claude Code users report +46K tokens (34K → 80K) just from enabling GitHub MCP; an empty-session context shows 82K tokens (41%) spent on MCP tool descriptions.

More tools also degrade selection: tool-selection accuracy drops from >90% with few tools to ~13.6% with many, and tool filtering alone restores it ~3x (43.1%, RAG-MCP benchmark, arXiv 2505.03275); Anthropic's internal eval shows +25pp accuracy from Tool Search over static schemas.

Today OMP's only lever is all-or-nothing per server (`disabledServers` / `enabled: false`) — "40 tools" or "0 tools". This is the missing middle: keep the heavy server available at a fraction of its context footprint.

## Why these names — feature parity

`enabledTools` / `disabledTools` reuses OMP's own server-level `enabledServers` / `disabledServers` vocabulary. Verified landscape (Aug 2026):

| Harness | Per-server filter | Glob support |
|---|---|---|
| **OMP (this PR)** | `enabledTools` + `disabledTools` (both sides) | picomatch: `*`, `?`, `[...]`, `{a,b}`; globs cross `/` — tool names are opaque strings |
| Goose (Block) | `available_tools` (allowlist; empty = all) | none — exact names |
| GitHub Copilot CLI | `tools: ["*"]` or exact names | bare `*` token only |
| LangChain (deepagents) | `allowedTools` / `disabledTools`, mutually exclusive | fnmatch `*`/`?`/`[...]`; no braces |
| Gemini CLI | `includeTools` / `excludeTools` | none; exclude wins |
| Qwen Code | `includeTools` / `excludeTools` (exact per server) | none per server |
| Claude Code | none per server — `permissions.deny` `mcp__<server>__*` | `*` after a literal server prefix |
| Roo Code / Windsurf / Antigravity | `disabledTools` (deny-only) | exact names |
| OpenCode / Devin / Zed | permission patterns / `tools: {name: bool}` map | `*`/`?` in permission layer only |
| Cline / Cursor / continue.dev / Junie | not shipped | — |

This is a minimum additive change for feature parity: both an allow side and a deny side per server with full picomatch globs — the glob gap only LangChain had, plus brace alternation no competitor ships. Servers that don't set the new fields behave exactly as before.

## Semantics

- Matched against **raw server-advertised tool names** (`tools/list`), not the `mcp__server_`-prefixed session names — a server rename never silently breaks the filter.
- Literal entries match exactly; glob metacharacters (`*`, `?`, `[...]`, `{a,b}`) use [picomatch](https://github.com/micromatch/picomatch) semantics (already in the dependency tree, now a direct dep). Picomatch treats `/` as a path separator and a leading `.` as a dotfile, while MCP tool names are opaque strings (`admin/delete`, `.hidden`), so both the pattern and the name are matched in the identifier domain `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` — every other character collapses to one `_` — with the raw name tested too so an entry written for a name's literal spelling still reaches it. Matching semantics are maintained upstream, not hand-rolled.
- Both set → `disabledTools` wins (deny subtracts from allow), mirroring server-level `disabledServers` > `enabledServers` and the ecosystem (Gemini/Qwen: exclude wins).
- Unknown entries are warned and ignored — a typo is loud; an upstream tool rename degrades to "filter ignored", not a dead server. A malformed pattern compiles to a never-matching matcher and surfaces as `unmatched` (warned) instead of disabling the server.
- OMP-specific fields, read from OMP-owned config sources (`.omp/mcp.json`, `~/.omp/agent/mcp.json`, root `mcp.json`/`.mcp.json`, OMP plugins) following the `requestIdFormat` scoping convention; configs translated from other tools ignore them. Validated by `parseMCPToolFilterEntry` (strict arrays; strings rejected, not CSV-split — comma globs like `"{create,delete}_*"` survive intact) and schema-enforced (array of non-empty unique strings).
- Aliases with the same filter members (any order/duplicates) still dedup to one connection — `isSameMCPConnection` compares normalized filter sets and keeps its existing auth/oauth guard.

## Architecture — filter at the reception boundary

Unlike the closed predecessors (#9516, #10335), the filter is applied at **one** place: `listTools` in `src/mcp/client.ts`, immediately after the `tools/list` response is assembled across pagination. The filtered subset is cached into `connection.tools`, which makes it the single source of truth for every downstream consumer:

- **Every registration path is covered by construction** — initial connect, concurrent startup, reconnect, and `tools/list_changed` refresh all call `listTools`, so excluded tools can never be restored into the session. No per-path filter re-application, no race between registration paths.
- **The tool cache stores the filtered set** — `toolCache.set` receives the post-filter list, and `hashConfig` includes the filter fields, so editing the filter invalidates the cache automatically. The deferred cached fallback (`DeferredMCPTool.fromTools`) cannot resurrect excluded tools.
- **Zero UI/controller leakage** — `/session` status, `/mcp test`, `/extensions` catalog, and runtime snapshots all read `connection.tools` or manager tools derived from it, so they all display the filtered set with titles and schemas intact — no bespoke per-surface reconciliation logic.
- **No lifecycle state machine changes** — a filter that excludes every advertised tool results in a connected server contributing 0 tools (resources/prompts stay available, per MCP's orthogonal capabilities), with a `logger.warn` diagnostic. Tools, resources, and prompts are independent server capabilities; an intentionally tool-less server is not a transport failure. No new connection-health state, no `failed`-while-transport-alive contradiction, no manager status-event rewrites.

## Implementation

- `src/mcp/tool-filter.ts` (new, 328 lines): pure picomatch-based filter + diagnostics; literal fast path; wildcard-token and name-length match-time bounds; malformed filters degrade to filter-off; no throwing control flow.
- `src/mcp/client.ts` (+6/-2 in `listTools`): apply the filter at reception and cache the filtered set.
- `src/capability/mcp.ts`: config fields, legacy conversion pass-through, and `isSameMCPConnection` dedup guard.
- Discovery: `builtin` / `mcp-json` / `omp-plugins` / `codex` (`enabled_tools`/`disabled_tools` map onto the same fields) parse the fields via `parseMCPToolFilters`; `src/mcp/config.ts` (Exa mount decision consults the filters), `src/mcp/name-sanitize.ts` (filter-domain sanitizer), `src/discovery/helpers.ts` (strict-array parsing + scalar expansion), `mcp-schema.json`, docs, CHANGELOG updated.

## Tests (69 new)

- `test/mcp/mcp-tool-filter.test.ts` (38) — allowlist, denylist, deny-subtracts-from-allow, unmatched reporting, glob semantics (star/question/braces/classes, escaped braces, malformed entries degrade to unmatched), the sanitized-name domain, negated-class behavior, filter-key normalization, definition/schema preservation.
- `test/mcp-tool-filter-reception.test.ts` (4) — integration against the reception boundary: allowlist filters and caches into `connection.tools`, deny-subtracts-from-allow, cached second call, all-excluding filter returns `[]` without disconnecting the transport.
- `test/mcp/config-tool-filter.test.ts` (8) — config-plumbing contract: filters survive `.omp/mcp.json` and root `.mcp.json` loaders, connection dedup keeps/resolves aliases by filter membership, and plugin-root placeholders stay literal in filter entries.
- `test/mcp/config-schema.test.ts` (5) — the bundled JSON schema accepts every documented shared server field on all three transports while still rejecting unknown and transport-conflicting keys.
- `test/mcp-exa-filter.test.ts` (+12) — Exa mount decision now consults the filters: an allowlist that selects only the native tool drops the server, a denylist that leaves a non-native tool reachable keeps it, and a name the server may really advertise (`constructor`) is never read as native.
- `test/discovery/codex-mcp-tool-filter.test.ts` (2) — Codex `enabled_tools`/`disabled_tools` map onto the same fields.

## Notes

- Third attempt after #9516 (closed for its hand-rolled fnmatch→regex translator — 4 review rounds consumed by translator defects) and #10335 (closed for filtering late in `MCPTool.fromTools`, which leaked unfiltered `connection.tools` into UI surfaces and forced a 24-file diff). This PR keeps the matcher-upstream decision and moves the filter to the earliest boundary, so the diff stays at 24 files.
- The issue's suggested "reject when both sets are configured" is deliberately not followed: the server level already resolves `disabledServers` > `enabledServers`, and Gemini/Qwen/LangChain all let deny subtract from allow.

Closes #6299
